### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Locating objects in common storage areas
Check common furniture pieces like shelves or cabinets first, as these are high-probability locations for household items.

### Verify object status before leaving a location
Always check your inventory using the "inventory" command to confirm you are holding the correct item before navigating away. If the action list does not show a "take" command, verify your position and proximity to the object, as you may need to move closer or "examine" the holder first to make the object interactable.

### Sequential object manipulation
Always follow the sequence of locating the object, picking it up, navigating to the destination, and then placing or moving the object to the target surface.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Verify Object States and Inventory
Before moving to the final destination, check the inventory to confirm the item is held, and if necessary, use the "examine" action or check the object's properties to verify it has been processed to the desired state (e.g., heated) before placing it on the target surface.

### Verify object status before leaving a location
Always check your inventory using the "inventory" command to confirm you are holding the correct item before navigating away. If the action list does not show a "take" command, verify your position and proximity to the object, as you may need to move closer or "examine" the holder first to make the object interactable.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Locating objects in common storage areas
Check common furniture pieces like shelves or cabinets first, as these are high-probability locations for household items.

### Update Search Scope to Include All Furniture Categories
If the standard search locations do not yield the target objects, perform a survey of all remaining furniture types in the environment. Broaden the search by systematically visiting furniture in a logical, geographic order rather than randomly switching between shelves and drawers.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

Before moving to the final destination, check the inventory to confirm the item is held, and if necessary, use the "examine" action or check the object's properties to verify it has been processed to the desired state (e.g., heated) before placing it on the target surface.

When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Re-evaluating environment upon status changes
If a task is not marked as complete after an action, verify the state of the destination and re-scan the environment to ensure no required objects were missed or dropped. Returning to previously visited locations is often necessary if the initial search was incomplete.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Analyze spatial descriptors carefully
If the object is not visible, consider that "under" might imply looking inside a closed container, beneath a piece of furniture, or requiring a specific interaction with the object acting as the reference point to reveal hidden items.

### Avoid repetitive interaction loops
If a repetitive action fails to reveal new information, stop repeating it immediately; instead, pivot to a different location or interaction method to avoid entering an infinite loop that wastes turns.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Analyze spatial descriptors carefully
If the object is not visible, consider that "under" might imply looking inside a closed container, beneath a piece of furniture, or requiring a specific interaction with the object acting as the reference point to reveal hidden items.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Avoid repetitive interaction loops
If a repetitive action fails to reveal new information, stop repeating it immediately; instead, pivot to a different location or interaction method to avoid entering an infinite loop that wastes turns.

When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

If the standard search locations do not yield the target objects, perform a survey of all remaining furniture types in the environment. Broaden the search by systematically visiting furniture in a logical, geographic order rather than randomly switching between shelves and drawers.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Container Accessibility
Simply standing near a closed drawer is insufficient; always perform an action to open containers if the contents are not immediately visible. Do not assume a location is devoid of items until you have interacted with it to reveal hidden contents.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

memory_context:
### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Container Interaction Workflow
First, navigate to the target container, then verify its state; if the container is closed, open it before attempting to place or move the held item inside.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Verify Container Accessibility
Simply standing near a closed drawer is insufficient; always perform an action to open containers if the contents are not immediately visible. Do not assume a location is devoid of items until you have interacted with it to reveal hidden contents.

Sequentially explore all likely storage containers (e.g., drawers, cabinets) and surface areas (e.g., tables, shelves) one by one. Check your inventory periodically to confirm if you have successfully acquired the item during your search.

Small objects are frequently left on open surfaces such as coffee tables, desks, or nightstands. When containers yield no results, search these flat surfaces before repeating or exhausting container searches.

Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

memory_context:
### Mandatory Cleaning Protocol
Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Container Accessibility
Simply standing near a closed drawer is insufficient; always perform an action to open containers if the contents are not immediately visible. Do not assume a location is devoid of items until you have interacted with it to reveal hidden contents.

### Avoid Redundant Searching
Instead of randomly revisiting cabinets in a loop, maintain a list of "checked" locations. Once a container (e.g., a specific cabinet or drawer) has been opened and inspected, mark it as searched to ensure your search process is linear and exhaustive rather than circular.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

memory_context:
### Locating and Identifying Environmental Landmarks
Before attempting to interact with the target object, perform an exhaustive scan of the scene to identify the required landmark. Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Interacting with Enclosed Containers
Always ensure the container is opened before attempting to move the object into it. If the container is closed, perform an 'open' action first to make the interior accessible.

### Container Verification
Before attempting to place an object into a container, verify the container's state by examining it or performing the placement action; if the container is closed, the system will typically handle the opening automatically or prompt you to do so.

### Verify Object States and Inventory
Before moving to the final destination, check the inventory to confirm the item is held, and if necessary, use the "examine" action or check the object's properties to verify it has been processed to the desired state (e.g., heated) before placing it on the target surface.

memory_context:
### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Managing Object Temperature
If an object is not at the required temperature, place it inside an appropriate thermal appliance (like a fridge for cooling or a microwave for heating) before moving it to the final destination. Ensure the appliance is open or accessible before attempting to change the temperature.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Comprehensive Room Scouting
Instead of repeatedly checking the same drawers or surfaces, systematically visit and examine every reachable piece of furniture, including countertops, sidetables, and all drawers within every dresser or cabinet. Keep a mental or scratchpad log of already searched containers to avoid redundant cycles.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

### Locating and Identifying Environmental Landmarks
Before attempting to interact with the target object, perform an exhaustive scan of the scene to identify the required landmark. Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

Before attempting to interact with two objects, confirm the precise location of both; if one is missing, prioritize searching for the object (the CD) until found, then bring it to the location of the other (the desklamp) to complete the interaction.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. Always ensure the container is opened before attempting to move the object into it. If the container is closed, perform an 'open' action first to make the interior accessible.

### Container Verification
Before attempting to place an object into a container, verify the container's state by examining it or performing the placement action; if the container is closed, the system will typically handle the opening automatically or prompt you to do so.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Standardizing Heating Procedures
After opening the appliance, place the item inside, close the appliance, and initiate the heating action if the device requires an explicit command to toggle its state.

### Container Interaction Workflow
Before placing an object into a container such as a drawer or cabinet, always verify if it is open and execute an "open" action if the container is currently closed.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

Instead of randomly revisiting cabinets in a loop, maintain a list of "checked" locations. Once a container (e.g., a specific cabinet or drawer) has been opened and inspected, mark it as searched to ensure your search process is linear and exhaustive rather than circular.

memory_context:
### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Heating perishable items
Locate a heating appliance, place the target object inside, and activate the appliance to change the object's state to "hot." Ensure the object is successfully processed before proceeding to the final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Contextual Object Inspection
Always ensure you open containers and examine their contents specifically rather than just navigating to them; an object is rarely "in" a cabinet if the cabinet door remains closed. If the agent repeatedly checks the same locations without success, re-evaluate if the object might be located on an open surface (like a table or countertop) instead of being stored away.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Heating Perishable Items
After placing an object in a heating appliance like a microwave or stove, you must explicitly use an activation action (such as "toggle" or "heat") to change the object's state; simply placing it inside is insufficient.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Heating perishable items
Locate a heating appliance, place the target object inside, and activate the appliance to change the object's state to "hot." Ensure the object is successfully processed before proceeding to the final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Troubleshooting Missing Placement Actions
If the "put" or "move to" action is unavailable despite holding an object, check if the receptacle needs to be opened first or if the object must be placed in a specific sub-compartment. Use "examine" on the container to reveal hidden states, such as a lid or door, that must be manipulated before the item can be inserted.

Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Object Property Verification
Before attempting to use an object, inspect it to determine its current state; if it does not meet the requirements, perform the necessary state-change action (such as cooling in a fridge) before proceeding to the final task step. If you do not have the object yet, prioritize searching in locations that naturally provide that state (e.g., the fridge for a "cool" item).

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Object Property Verification
Before attempting to use an object, inspect it to determine its current state; if it does not meet the requirements, perform the necessary state-change action (such as cooling in a fridge) before proceeding to the final task step. If you do not have the object yet, prioritize searching in locations that naturally provide that state (e.g., the fridge for a "cool" item).

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Task Sequencing for State Changes
Break the task into distinct phases: locate, process (e.g., cool/heat), and place. Always complete the process phase while holding the object or being at the processing station before moving to the final placement area.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

Always ensure you open containers and examine their contents specifically rather than just navigating to them; an object is rarely "in" a cabinet if the cabinet door remains closed. If the agent repeatedly checks the same locations without success, re-evaluate if the object might be located on an open surface (like a table or countertop) instead of being stored away.

### Mandatory Cleaning Protocol
Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Contextual Object Inspection
Always ensure you open containers and examine their contents specifically rather than just navigating to them; an object is rarely "in" a cabinet if the cabinet door remains closed. If the agent repeatedly checks the same locations without success, re-evaluate if the object might be located on an open surface (like a table or countertop) instead of being stored away.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

memory_context:
### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Heating Perishable Items
After placing an object in a heating appliance like a microwave or stove, you must explicitly use an activation action (such as "toggle" or "heat") to change the object's state; simply placing it inside is insufficient.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Heating perishable items
Locate a heating appliance, place the target object inside, and activate the appliance to change the object's state to "hot." Ensure the object is successfully processed before proceeding to the final destination.

memory_context:
### Mandatory Cleaning Protocol
Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Contextual Object Inspection
Always ensure you open containers and examine their contents specifically rather than just navigating to them; an object is rarely "in" a cabinet if the cabinet door remains closed. If the agent repeatedly checks the same locations without success, re-evaluate if the object might be located on an open surface (like a table or countertop) instead of being stored away.

memory_context:
### Mandatory Cleaning Protocol
Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Prioritize visible scanning of the environment
Before initiating a cabinet-by-cabinet search, perform a "look" or "scan" command to check for objects placed on surfaces like countertops, tables, or stoves. Frequently, the target object might be sitting out in the open, making a deep search of enclosed storage unnecessary.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Perform Sequence of Heating Actions
To heat an object, ensure it is inside the appliance, close the appliance door, and then perform the specific activation action (like "toggle" or "heat"). Do not skip the activation step, as merely placing an object inside an appliance will not change its state.

### Verifying Task Requirements
Before attempting to interact with two objects, confirm the precise location of both; if one is missing, prioritize searching for the object (the CD) until found, then bring it to the location of the other (the desklamp) to complete the interaction.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Systematic Room Exploration
Instead of repeatedly visiting the same locations (like a desk or table) without a strategy, maintain a list of visited locations and prioritize searching unexplored containers, drawers, and shelves until all potential storage areas are checked.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Prioritizing Specialized Storage
If an object must meet a specific condition like being "cool," prioritize checking the fridge first, as it may contain the item in the desired state, saving the time and effort required to cool it manually later. If the object is not in its expected functional storage, proceed to a systematic search of general storage areas.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

memory_context:
### Locating and Identifying Environmental Landmarks
Before attempting to interact with the target object, perform an exhaustive scan of the scene to identify the required landmark. Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

### Verifying Task Requirements
Before attempting to interact with two objects, confirm the precise location of both; if one is missing, prioritize searching for the object (the CD) until found, then bring it to the location of the other (the desklamp) to complete the interaction.

### Use the Object First, Then Examine
Before attempting to examine an object, ensure the secondary object (the tool) is fully activated. If the environment returns "Nothing happens," try toggling the state of the tool (e.g., turn it on/off) and re-executing the interaction to ensure the state change is registered by the system.

### Use specific examine actions on target objects
When tasked to look at a specific object, always look for an "examine [object]" action in the admissible actions list. If the specific "examine" action is missing, try to navigate closer to the object or interact with it until the specific action becomes available rather than performing a broad surface examination.

### Maintain original object placement for positional tasks
If a task requires an object to be observed in a specific location (like under a lamp), picking it up or moving it will likely invalidate the required spatial state. Only interact with the object in a way that allows you to observe it while keeping it in its original location.

Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

Before attempting to interact with the target object, perform an exhaustive scan of the scene to identify the required landmark. Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

Before attempting to interact with two objects, confirm the precise location of both; if one is missing, prioritize searching for the object (the CD) until found, then bring it to the location of the other (the desklamp) to complete the interaction.

### Verify Task Conditions Before Execution
Confirm the existence and state of all required items (the bowl and the desklamp) before proceeding to the final action. If a prerequisite like turning on a lamp is required for an examination, perform that action immediately after locating the items.

### Use the Object First, Then Examine
Before attempting to examine an object, ensure the secondary object (the tool) is fully activated. If the environment returns "Nothing happens," try toggling the state of the tool (e.g., turn it on/off) and re-executing the interaction to ensure the state change is registered by the system.

### Use specific examine actions on target objects
When tasked to look at a specific object, always look for an "examine [object]" action in the admissible actions list. If the specific "examine" action is missing, try to navigate closer to the object or interact with it until the specific action becomes available rather than performing a broad surface examination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verifying Task Requirements
Before attempting to interact with two objects, confirm the precise location of both; if one is missing, prioritize searching for the object (the CD) until found, then bring it to the location of the other (the desklamp) to complete the interaction.

### Use Environment Observation to Plan Search
Instead of searching every drawer in a single furniture piece, scan the entire room for other types of containers (e.g., cabinets, shelves, sidetables) or check for visual cues in the room description that might indicate where the object is kept.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Prioritize Visual Scan Before Interaction
Before spending steps opening every drawer, use "look" commands or scan your current view to see if the objects are sitting in plain sight on a surface, which is often more efficient than checking every internal storage compartment.

memory_context:
### Mandatory Cleaning Protocol
Even if the object does not appear visibly dirty, treat it as "dirty" by default and carry it to a sinkbasin to use the clean interaction. This guarantees that the "clean" state requirement is met before the item is placed in its final destination.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

If an object is not at the required temperature, place it inside an appropriate thermal appliance (like a fridge for cooling or a microwave for heating) before moving it to the final destination. Ensure the appliance is open or accessible before attempting to change the temperature.

Before attempting to use an object, inspect it to determine its current state; if it does not meet the requirements, perform the necessary state-change action (such as cooling in a fridge) before proceeding to the final task step. Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. ### Systematic Search for Multiple Items
Instead of repeatedly visiting the same locations (like the same countertop or hanger), maintain a mental list of locations already searched and prioritize unexplored storage containers like cabinets or drawers. This prevents getting stuck in a cycle of checking empty surfaces while the remaining items are hidden in closed or un-searched containers.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Heating Perishable Items
After placing an object in a heating appliance like a microwave or stove, you must explicitly use an activation action (such as "toggle" or "heat") to change the object's state; simply placing it inside is insufficient.

### Prioritize visible scanning of the environment
Before initiating a cabinet-by-cabinet search, perform a "look" or "scan" command to check for objects placed on surfaces like countertops, tables, or stoves. Frequently, the target object might be sitting out in the open, making a deep search of enclosed storage unnecessary.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Maintain original object placement for positional tasks
If a task requires an object to be observed in a specific location (like under a lamp), picking it up or moving it will likely invalidate the required spatial state. Only interact with the object in a way that allows you to observe it while keeping it in its original location.

### Understanding "Look At" Requirements
Do not assume that general surface examinations (like "examine desk") satisfy the requirement to "look at" a specific target object. If a specific "examine [object]" action is not available, try to look at the object using navigation or orientation adjustments (e.g., "look") while positioned directly in front of the target.

### Locating and Identifying Environmental Landmarks
Before attempting to interact with the target object, perform an exhaustive scan of the scene to identify the required landmark. Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

### Interpret "under" as a spatial relationship for object placement
Instead of searching for the object already in that location, identify the object you need to interact with, pick it up, and use the 'put' command to place it on the same surface as the target landmark. If the system does not support a specific "under" command, placing the object on the surface near or at the location of the landmark is the standard way to satisfy the spatial constraint.

### Use specific examine actions on target objects
When tasked to look at a specific object, always look for an "examine [object]" action in the admissible actions list. If the specific "examine" action is missing, try to navigate closer to the object or interact with it until the specific action becomes available rather than performing a broad surface examination.

When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

### Efficient Inventory Management
Before attempting to place multiple items, check your current inventory and the immediate environment to minimize trips. If your carrying capacity is limited, prioritize clearing the current load before retrieving the next set of items.

### Distinguishing Similar Object Classes
Carefully distinguish between object types (e.g., "spraybottle" versus "soapbottle") by reading the observation labels precisely. Do not assume an object is the target simply because it is in the same category or location as other target items; verify the object name before taking it.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Verifying Task Requirements
Before attempting to interact with two objects, confirm the precise location of both; if one is missing, prioritize searching for the object (the CD) until found, then bring it to the location of the other (the desklamp) to complete the interaction.

### Direct Item Relocation
Once the target item is in your possession, navigate directly to the destination furniture and use the put/move action to place the item onto the surface area.

Before attempting to place multiple items, check your current inventory and the immediate environment to minimize trips. If your carrying capacity is limited, prioritize clearing the current load before retrieving the next set of items.

If you encounter one of the required items while searching for others, secure it immediately and bring it to the target destination. This clears your inventory for the next search and reduces the distance traveled when you find the subsequent items.

### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Distinguishing Similar Object Classes
Carefully distinguish between object types (e.g., "spraybottle" versus "soapbottle") by reading the observation labels precisely. Do not assume an object is the target simply because it is in the same category or location as other target items; verify the object name before taking it.

### Mandatory cleaning before placement
Before placing an object into a clean area like a toilet or basin, always verify if it requires cleaning; if so, navigate to a sink and perform the cleaning action first to ensure compliance with hygiene protocols.

memory_context:
### Decompose "Hot" Object Tasks
When a task specifies a processed object (e.g., "hot plate"), recognize that this requires a two-step process: finding the base object (the plate) and then performing the appropriate interaction to change its state (e.g., placing it on a stove burner or in a microwave). Do not treat the final state as an attribute of the object's initial location.

### Object Property Verification
Before attempting to use an object, inspect it to determine its current state; if it does not meet the requirements, perform the necessary state-change action (such as cooling in a fridge) before proceeding to the final task step. If you do not have the object yet, prioritize searching in locations that naturally provide that state (e.g., the fridge for a "cool" item).

### Prioritizing Specialized Storage
If an object must meet a specific condition like being "cool," prioritize checking the fridge first, as it may contain the item in the desired state, saving the time and effort required to cool it manually later. If the object is not in its expected functional storage, proceed to a systematic search of general storage areas.

### Verify Object Properties Before Interaction
Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

### Prioritize visible scanning of the environment
Before initiating a cabinet-by-cabinet search, perform a "look" or "scan" command to check for objects placed on surfaces like countertops, tables, or stoves. Frequently, the target object might be sitting out in the open, making a deep search of enclosed storage unnecessary.

memory_context:
### Use "put" action to complete object placement
Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Perform Sequence of Heating Actions
To heat an object, ensure it is inside the appliance, close the appliance door, and then perform the specific activation action (like "toggle" or "heat"). Do not skip the activation step, as merely placing an object inside an appliance will not change its state.

### Systematic Search for Multiple Items
Instead of repeatedly visiting the same locations (like the same countertop or hanger), maintain a mental list of locations already searched and prioritize unexplored storage containers like cabinets or drawers. This prevents getting stuck in a cycle of checking empty surfaces while the remaining items are hidden in closed or un-searched containers.

### Establishing Correct Spatial Relationships
If the object is not already in the required position, pick up the object and use spatial placement actions (like 'put' or 'move') to place it correctly relative to the identified landmark. After placing it, confirm the new state by examining the object or the surface to ensure the condition is met.

### Prioritize "put" actions over continued searching
Do not continue searching for new locations if you are already in possession of the required item and have a suitable container available. If a container is open and empty, it is likely a valid target, so focus on successfully placing the held item instead of exploring further cabinets.

Before attempting to use an item, check its current state (e.g., using 'examine'). If the object does not meet the specified condition, perform the necessary preparatory action (such as placing it in a fridge to cool it) before proceeding to the final task.

If an object must meet a specific condition like being "cool," prioritize checking the fridge first, as it may contain the item in the desired state, saving the time and effort required to cool it manually later. If the object is not in its expected functional storage, proceed to a systematic search of general storage areas.

Many environments require an explicit "put [object] in [receptacle]" command. If the "put" action is missing from your admissible actions list, ensure you are standing directly in front of the target, that the container is open, and that you are looking at it; if the command still does not appear, try interacting with the container (e.g., "examine") to refresh the state.

### Prioritize visible scanning of the environment
Before initiating a cabinet-by-cabinet search, perform a "look" or "scan" command to check for objects placed on surfaces like countertops, tables, or stoves. Frequently, the target object might be sitting out in the open, making a deep search of enclosed storage unnecessary.

If a task requires an object to be observed in a specific location (like under a lamp), picking it up or moving it will likely invalidate the required spatial state. Only interact with the object in a way that allows you to observe it while keeping it in its original location.

### Understanding "Look At" Requirements
Do not assume that general surface examinations (like "examine desk") satisfy the requirement to "look at" a specific target object. If a specific "examine [object]" action is not available, try to look at the object using navigation or orientation adjustments (e.g., "look") while positioned directly in front of the target.

Before interacting with target objects, scan the environment for the required landmark (e.g., the desklamp) to confirm its location. Do not assume a common piece of furniture automatically contains the specific landmark; verify its presence in the observation list first.

### Locating and Identifying Environmental Landmarks
Before attempting to interact with the target object, perform an exhaustive scan of the scene to identify the required landmark. Do not assume the landmark is obvious; examine surfaces and furniture until the landmark (e.g., a lamp, a container, or a piece of furniture) is explicitly listed in the observation.

### Interpret "under" as a spatial relationship for object placement
Instead of searching for the object already in that location, identify the object you need to interact with, pick it up, and use the 'put' command to place it on the same surface as the target landmark. If the system does not support a specific "under" command, placing the object on the surface near or at the location of the landmark is the standard way to satisfy the spatial constraint.
